catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-mickiewi:
Adam Mickiewicz was born near Novogrodek, Lithuania, in 1798 and died at Constantinople in 1855. He studied at Novogrodek until 1815, then entered Vilna University, where he pursued German and English romantic poetry with great zeal. A love for Marya Wereszczak, thwarted, roused his genius rather than quenching it. After becoming a professor at Kovno in 1819, he published his first poems in two volumes in 1822 and 1823.

Those volumes held Dziady, the Ancestors, marking romanticism's first appearance in Poland. They also held ballads and romances setting Lithuanian folklore forth with power, and Grazyna, a lyric epic of real simplicity and majesty. Persecution then changed his genius's current: imprisoned with a student society that had never dreamed of insurrection, he turned from disappointed love to suffering patriotism. Exiled to Russia in 1824, he left Lithuania forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-anton:
Charles Antoniewicz was a Polish Jesuit and missionary born at Lwów in 1807 and dead in 1852. His father was a nobleman and lawyer. He grew up on the estate at Skwarzawa. He studied law at Lwów, giving time to philology until he spoke German, French, Italian, and English besides Polish. He gathered material on the Armenians in Poland and wrote poetry in Polish and German. He finished law with the highest distinction in 1827, toured Austria and Rumania, and served under General Dwernicki in the insurrection of 1830-31.

In 1833 he married his cousin Sophia Nikorowicz and settled at Skwarzawa. His five children died, then his wife, who took religious vows on her deathbed and begged him to enter an order. With the counsel of his director, Father Frederic Rinn, he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Stara Wies in September 1839. He stayed a Jesuit missionary until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-szymono:
Szymonowicz, also known by the Latin name Simonides, was born at Lemberg in 1558 and died in 1629. He studied first at Lemberg, then at the Cracow Academy, then abroad in the Netherlands and France. Returning home, he tutored privately, teaching Sobieski's father and the son of John Zolkiewski, who took Moscow. He enjoyed close ties with John Zamoyski, whose son he also educated. In 1614 he retired to the country until his death. He never married.

He may be called the last of the Polish Humanists, in erudition and in the character of his creations alike. He spent most of his life writing Latin poems. His best include odes to Zamoyski, a paraphrase of Joel dedicated to Clement VIII, and two dramas, Penthesilea and Castus Joseph. His fame rests chiefly on his Idyls of 1614, the first and still the best poems of their kind in Polish, faithfully following the classical models.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-bakocz:
Thomas Bakocz, cardinal and statesman of Hungary, rose from a low-born family in Szatmar county to become the real ruler of his country. Born about 1442, he studied at Szatmar, Cracow, Ferrara and Padua, then entered the court of King Matthias, where he served as secretary and royal chancellor's deputy. After Matthias died in 1490 he helped choose Ladislaus II as king and became chancellor of the realm.

Bakocz steered foreign policy with skill, making Venice the pivot of his alliances and sealing useful treaties with other powers. He also became Archbishop of Esztergom and a cardinal, and used his wealth to endow his family and build chapels, including a Renaissance chapel at Gran where he was buried. He died in 1521 with his personal conduct unblemished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zircz:
Zircz is the Cistercian abbey in Hungary's Veszprém diocese, also called Boccon. Its early history is obscure in names and dates, since it appears under both titles, and whether Zircz and Boccon were separate abbeys cannot now be determined. Most probably Béla III founded it in 1182, as the monastic domain was formerly a royal farm. Besides this grant, on which the city of Zircz now stands, many donations made the nascent abbey soon one of the country's most celebrated. It was rich in temporal possessions and in fervour and religious regularity.

In 1609 Canon Michael Monoszloy acquired it; in 1659 it passed to Kolweiss, Abbot of Lilienfeld, who appointed Martin Ujfalusy abbot in 1660. Expelled in 1810, the community was restored in 1814 under Abbot Antonius Dreta, under whom Pilis and Pasto joined Zircz, and in 1878 Szentgotthard too. Zircz now holds 105 priests, 35 clerics, and 11 novices.
